options.title: The Pump Handle That Changed Medicine #Shorts
options.description:
In 1854, Dr. John Snow mapped London's Soho cholera outbreak to a single water pump handle, helping launch modern epidemiology.

Sources:
- Snow, John. 'On the Mode of Communication of Cholera', 1855.
- Vinten-Johansen et al., 'Cholera, Chloroform, and the Science of Medicine: A Life of John Snow', Oxford University Press.
script_lines: In 1854, a single water pump handle in London changed the history of medicine forever.
As cholera struck Soho, physician John Snow suspected contaminated water, not foul air, was spreading the illness.
He plotted sick households on a street map, tracing the cluster directly to the Broad Street pump.
Snow persuaded local leaders to remove the wooden pump handle, disabling the contaminated well.
The neighborhood outbreak rapidly subsided, laying the foundation for modern public health tracking.

options.title: The 1904 Olympic Marathon Car Fraud #Shorts
options.description:
At the 1904 St. Louis Olympics, Fred Lorz crossed the finish line first after riding 11 miles inside a car.

Sources:
- International Olympic Committee (IOC) Historical Archives, 1904 St. Louis Games.
- Matthews, George R., 'America's First Olympic Games', University of Missouri Press.
script_lines: The 1904 Olympic marathon winner rode to victory inside a nine-horsepower automobile.
American runner Fred Lorz cramped nine miles into the race and flagged down his manager's car.
He waved at spectators for eleven miles before the car broke down, prompting him to walk back onto the track.
Lorz crossed the finish line first and posed for photos with Alice Roosevelt before officials uncovered the truth.
He claimed it was just a prank, leaving gold to Thomas Hicks, who ran while consuming egg whites and strychnine.

options.title: Tycho Brahe's Silver Nose #Shorts
options.description:
Famous 16th-century astronomer Tycho Brahe lost the bridge of his nose in a duel over mathematics and wore a metal prosthetic for life.

Sources:
- Christianson, John Robert, 'On Tycho's Island: Tycho Brahe and His Assistants', Cambridge University Press.
- Danish National Museum archaeological analysis of Tycho Brahe's remains (2012).
script_lines: In 1566, a famous astronomer lost his nose in a sword duel over a math equation.
Twenty-year-old Danish nobleman Tycho Brahe argued with his cousin about who was the superior mathematician.
The quarrel ended in a duel in pitch darkness, where Tycho lost the bridge of his nose.
For the rest of his life, Tycho wore a custom prosthetic forged from silver and gold alloy.
He carried a small container of adhesive paste everywhere to keep his metallic nose glued in place.
